extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, communication students, researchers, and practitioners involved in organizational crisis response
extracted.subtask_description: General guidance and evaluative principles for preparing for, responding to, and learning from organizational crises, including theory-driven strategy selection, tactical recommendations for social media and press releases, and post-crisis follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-crisis preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing ahead of time for crisis management in an effort to prevent a future crisis from occurring (also called the prodromal crisis stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and collect information about crisis risks specific to the organization; create a crisis management plan that assigns who will handle specific aspects of a crisis; conduct exercises to test the plan at least annually; prepare press release templates for the public relations team; prepare a "dark (unpublished) page" on the organization's website to activate as an authoritative source; define the chain of command for dissemination of information; organize a rapid response crisis communications team and train all individuals who will help with the actual response; focus on detecting and identifying possible risks in advance. (Examples: national Xenokratis/Egelados plans.)

rubrics_metrics.name: In-crisis response: initial critical response and reputation repair
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-crisis information and plans to react to an actual crisis through an early initial response and subsequent reputation repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial critical response must occur early, and provide precise and correct information; provide constant updates to keep the public safe (example: Japan agencies' post-2011 updates). Reputation repair requires taking responsibility as appropriate and proposing sufficient reimbursement for damages to affected parties. If pre-crisis data are wrong, timing alone cannot make up for incorrect substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-crisis review and follow-up (Coombs' five steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities after the crisis is resolved to learn, follow up, and integrate lessons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver all information promised to stakeholders as soon as known; keep stakeholders updated on recovery efforts and corrective measures and investigation progress; analyze the crisis management effort for lessons and integrate those lessons into the system; scan Internet channels for online memorials; consult with victims and families about the organization's role in anniversaries or memorials. Provide follow-up crisis messages as necessary and dissect successes and failures to change organization practices or procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) — strategy selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select crisis response strategies according to crisis type and stakeholders' attributions of responsibility; SCCT is audience-oriented and focuses on stakeholders' perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess crisis type and degree of attributed responsibility before choosing strategies. SCCT offers strategies such as denial, scapegoat, attack the accuser, excuse, justification, ingratiation, concern, compassion, regret, and apology. The effectiveness of a response strategy depends on the nature of the crisis and the degree of responsibility attributed to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base response components (Coombs) — instructing information + care
rubrics_metrics.description: Two halves of the base response to a crisis: instructing information and care response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All victims/potential victims should receive instructing information (e.g., recall instructions) and an expression of sympathy plus information about corrective actions and trauma counseling when needed (care response). For crises with minimal attribution of responsibility and no intensifying factors, these two are sufficient. Depending on attribution and intensifying factors, add excuse/justification, compensation, and/or apology strategies. Compensation is used when victims suffer serious harm. Reminder and ingratiation strategies may supplement any response. Denial and attack-the-accuser strategies are best used only for rumor and challenge crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate response and timing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat crisis response strategy and crisis timing strategy as integrated components of crisis management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is critical: delays or inappropriate responses can worsen the crisis. Combine pre-crisis preparation, crisis identification, assessment, and communication when developing plans. Practical recommendations include creating a crisis plan that integrates response and timing strategies, conducting regular crisis simulations and rehearsals, and communicating with stakeholders throughout the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benoit's image repair strategies (five major strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of response categories organizations can use to protect image during a crisis: deny, evade responsibility, reduce offensiveness, corrective action, and mortification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denial: simple denial or shifting blame (scapegoating). Evasion of responsibility: provocation, defeasibility, accident, good intentions. Reducing offensiveness: bolstering, minimizing, differentiation, transcending, attacking the accuser, offering compensation. Corrective action: promise to correct the problem and prevent recurrence (may rebuild reputation). Mortification: confessing wrongdoing and asking for forgiveness; often paired with corrective action. Note risks: scapegoating can create long-term negative consequences and loss of trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-mediated crisis communication (SMCC) model — platform & message form factors
rubrics_metrics.description: How social networks, blogs, and platform form influence crisis communication choices and tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five factors influence communication during crises: crisis origin, crisis type, infrastructure, message strategy, and message form. Use social media analytics to monitor topic and sentiment evolution in real time to anticipate public reactions, detect misinformation early, and adjust outreach. Platform differences matter: Twitter emphasizes timing and updates (use for early information and constant updates to limit rumors); Instagram requires visual communication guidelines and platform-specific policies. Establish platform-specific procedures in advance. Consider source credibility: experts often receive more favorable reactions; communicator identity (including gender) shapes audience interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated Crisis Mapping (ICM) — emotional mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and map stakeholders' emotional responses during crises to tailor messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICM assumes people continuously interpret their emotions during a crisis. Anxiety is often the default emotion, though anger, fright, and sadness may dominate depending on crisis nature. Monitor emotional trajectories and adapt messages to address dominant emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covariation-based approach to attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply consensus, distinctiveness, and consistency dimensions to anticipate stakeholder causal attributions and select information strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Kelley’s covariation principle for crisis situations: conceptualize consensus, distinctiveness, and consistency to predict whether stakeholders will make organizational, entity, or circumstance attributions, which then inform responsibility perceptions and reputation evaluations; deduce communication strategies from these attribution patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse of renewal — forward-looking and ethical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize learning from the crisis, ethical and prospective communication, and effective organizational rhetoric to enter a post-crisis renewal phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the discourse of renewal framework to focus on organizational learning, ethical communication, and prospective (future-oriented) messaging rather than solely defensive tactics when moving from crisis to opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical Arena Theory (RAT) — multi-vocal coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and manage the multi-voiced rhetorical arena where corporations, political actors, activists, experts, media, and others communicate and co-construct the crisis dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand patterns of interaction among various voices; monitor and, where possible, engage in the rhetorical arena since multiple actors will shape public meaning. RAT focuses on interactions between voices rather than single-actor messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealing thunder (proactive disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proactively disclose negative information about a problem before external sources do (“stealing thunder”), to minimize reputational damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research suggests proactive disclosure can minimize reputational loss; effectiveness is moderated by perceived organizational transparency. Organizations should weigh risks and benefits, consider timing and content, and be perceived as transparent for greater effectiveness. Develop crisis plans that include proactive communication options and transparency measures; study examples like Johnson & Johnson (Tylenol) and Toyota.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility and communicator characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of the message source and communicator attributes affect public reactions to crisis messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts tend to receive more favorable reactions because of perceived objectivity; politicians are often seen as less trustworthy. Communicator identity (including gender) shapes audience interpretation—research shows gender differences in early and later crisis reactions. Factor communicator credibility into channel and spokesperson selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis fatigue management
rubrics_metrics.description: Address stakeholder cognitive and emotional exhaustion from repeated or prolonged crisis exposure in the digital age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce message saturation, pace communications, prioritize clarity and empathy, and segment audiences during prolonged or repeated crises to maintain attentiveness and behavioral compliance. Adjust strategies to avoid overwhelming stakeholders and undermining long-term trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI in crisis communication — capabilities and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate AI tools for monitoring, prediction, and rapid message generation, while accounting for ethical and credibility concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI/ML can enable real-time sentiment analysis, misinformation tracking, automated messaging, satellite imagery and propagation prediction for natural disasters, and targeted marketing resilience. Maintain a human-in-the-loop for empathy, credibility, and accountability; be mindful of transparency, bias, and accountability in automated responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare press-release templates and authoritative online pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-write press release templates and prepare an unpublished authoritative web page to deploy during crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having templates expedites accurate initial messaging. A pre-prepared "dark page" can be activated to serve as the authoritative source for updates. Ensure templates and pages are reviewed, updated, and integrated into incident command and chain-of-command procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define chain of command and rapid response team roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish who will disseminate information and who will perform which communication tasks during a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document responsibilities across central, regional, and local levels where relevant; ensure all team members are trained; maintain clear escalation and approval paths so that responses are timely and coherent.
